chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Muhammad al-Asadi, from Salim ibn Mukram, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

The financial state of a man from the companions of the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) became difficult, so his wife said to him, 'If only you would go to the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) and ask him.' So he came to the Prophet (peace be upon him). When the Prophet (peace be upon him) saw him, he said: 'The one who asks us, we give to him, and the one who manages without (asking), Allah enriches him.'

The man said, 'He did not mean anyone apart from me.' So he returned to his wife and informed her. She said, 'The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) is a human being, so inform him of it.' So he went to him. When the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) saw him, he said: 'The one who asks us, we give to him, and the one who manages without (asking), Allah enriches him,' to the extent that the man did that three times.

Then the man went away, borrowed a pickaxe, went to the mountain, climbed it, and cut firewood. Then he brought it and sold it for half a Mudd of fine flour. He returned with it and ate it. Then he went the next day and brought more than that and sold it. He did not cease working and gathering until he bought a pickaxe. Then he gathered until he bought two young camels and a slave. Then he became wealthy to the extent that he became affluent.

So he came to the Prophet (peace be upon him) and informed him of how he had come to ask him and how he had heard the Prophet (peace be upon him). The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'I told you, the one who asks us, we give to him, and the one who manages without (asking), Allah enriches him.'

key_terms.اسْتَغْنَى: To manage without needing others; self-sufficiency

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic perspective on self-reliance versus asking for charity?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi illustrates the nuanced Shia understanding of *istighna* (self-sufficiency), distinguishing between the dignity of active labor and the humility of accepting charity. The companion’s repeated inquiries highlight the Prophet’s pedagogical method of guiding individuals toward economic independence through effort rather than passive reliance on alms. This narrative underscores the virtue of *istighna* as a spiritual and material state achieved through diligent work, a key theme in Twelver Shi'ite ethical teachings.
